blocks.content: A .dockerignore file excludes files and directories from the build context before Docker even sees them, syntactically close to .gitignore, but with real consequences for build speed and image security.

Before the build context is packaged and sent to the daemon, Docker checks it against any patterns listed in .dockerignore, and excludes matching files entirely, they are never sent, never visible to any COPY or ADD instruction.

blocks.alt: Filtering happens before the context is even sent

blocks.content: Patterns support wildcards (*.log for any log file), directory exclusions (node_modules/), and negation (!important.log to re-include something an earlier broader pattern excluded).

This is not just about speed, excluding files like .env means a careless COPY . . genuinely cannot pull secrets into the image, because they were never even part of the context Docker had access to in the first place. Contrast this with just remembering not to COPY them individually, which is one missed line away from a real leak.

blocks.alt: Secrets excluded from the context can never end up in the image

blocks.content: Every build sends the entire (filtered) context up front, before the first instruction even runs, exactly as covered in the Build Context topic. A lean, well-filtered context means less to send and a faster build start, every single time.

blocks.alt: A smaller context is faster to send, on every build

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: .dockerignore filters the build context before Docker even sees the excluded files, they are never reachable by COPY or ADD.
Beyond speed, this is a genuine security control, excluding secret files keeps them out of the image even if a Dockerfile line is careless.
